newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. historian plays down Holocaust row with Swiss.
newsitem.headline: U.S. historian plays down Holocaust row with Swiss.

text.p: A U.S. government historian who helped compile a critical report on Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre with ties to Nazi Germany sought on Friday to defuse a row the study has triggered with Berne.

State Department historian William Slany, who oversaw compilation of information in the 200-page report, stressed at a seminar in the Swiss parliament that the preliminary study was based on a "tentative analysis" and was "an account from a strictly American official perspective".

"It is by no means meant to be judgemental," Slany said, noting the report published in May contained information based mainly on U.S. sources, while other potentially valuable records were not included.
But Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti reiterated Berne's concerns about remarks in the report's foreword, which was written by U.S. Under-secretary of Commerce Stuart Eisenstat.

"It is stated in the foreword that Switzerland, by reason of its exports and its financial transactions with Germany, contributed to prolonging the war. However, the body of the report contains not a single element which bears out this statement," Cotti said.
"A foreword is not a summary," Slany countered.
"We recognise that Eisenstat was addressing the issues which had not been completely taken up in any detail."

The Eizenstat report charged that the Swiss bought gold from Germany that was looted from occupied countries or taken from the teeth of Holocaust victims. Swiss officials say they have no evidence Switzerland knew at the time the gold was looted.
The foreword also took issue with the concept of neutrality adopted by Switzerland and other nations such as Argentina, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
It said they were slow to acknowledge their moral obligations to fight fascism during World War Two.

"As regards the consequence of Swiss neutrality, our impression in reviewing the records for the report was that at the time, in the heat of war, the American officials, especially high-ranking officials, were concerned that any effort that contributed to the war effort on the part of Germany was prolonging the war," Slany said.
Thomas Borer, the Swiss diplomat handling Berne's response to charges over its wartime record, told Reuters he believed Slany's remarks cast a more positive light on Switzerland's role.
"Mr Slany has, in cautious words, took distance from this foreword on behalf of the U.S. government. I think this is a very important development," he said.
Jean-Pierre Roth, vice-chairman of the Swiss National Bank, said as well that the U.S. government was partly at fault for leading the Swiss into gold dealings with Nazi Germany.

Swiss officials have said that they needed to buy gold to maintain the gold parity with the Swiss franc during the war, fearing they would otherwise face a repeat of the sharp inflation seen during World War One.
Roth said that a U.S. government decision to freeze Swiss gold held in the U.S. Federal Reserve caused Switzerland to turn to Germany to supply gold.

Switzerland, which had a trade surplus with the U.S. starting in the early 1940s, found itself having to mop up excess Swiss currency, and one way to do this was to sell gold to its citizens in exchange.
"The U.S. forced us to play into Germany's hands," he said.
Borer agreed.

"This is a fair assessment. A lot of Swiss historians have said that by freezing Swiss assets, by treating Switzerland as an enemy country, the Swiss were pushed into the arms of the Nazis. And this made our survival much more difficult. This shows how complicated the situation was," Borer said.
